skyline.text: How the means of pro­duc­tion landed on Amit Varma’s lap­top
Ajay Shah on the fail­ures that mil­i­tary se­crecy hides
Johan Norberg on the free mar­kets be­hind Nordic wel­fare states

masthead.footnote: *There’s a paid version, but not necessary. Page 3

brief.head: Weak and too busy
brief.text: Amit Varma re­called Francis Fukuyama’s two axes, scope and strength[[x7]][[x8]]. The ideal is a strong state with lim­ited scope; India, he said, has a weak state that does too much. {026-C02}

brief.head: Words in disguise
brief.text: Economics re­pur­poses plain English words such as mar­ket fail­ure, pub­lic good and moral haz­ard[[x9]], Ajay Shah said. They seem “se­duc­tively ac­ces­si­ble”, but each is a tech­ni­cal term. {026-C06}

brief.head: Knowledge is hard
brief.text: Utilitarian thinkers as­sume knowl­edge is easy, Amit Varma said. Anyone who claims free­dom isn’t work­ing should face “a re­ally high bar of proof”. {026-C07}

brief.head: Even if you don’t care
brief.text: Suppose you value order or tra­di­tion, not lib­erty, Ajay Shah said. Even then, a base­line of free­dom and a state con­fined to mar­ket fail­ure is the path to pros­per­ity. {026-C08}

brief.head: Four-word mantra
brief.text: Amit Varma’s ques­tion for any prob­lem in so­ci­ety is “Where is the co­er­cion?” Find the co­er­cion, he said, and you find the root of the prob­lem. {026-C10}

thought.label: Thought for the day

thought.who: Amit Varma, quoting *Yes Minister*, or was it *Yes Prime Minister*, on the urge to act

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on the limits of the state
lead.head: Freedom first, state on probation

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 26

body: Leave peo­ple alone by de­fault. Let the state in only where it can make some peo­ple bet­ter off with­out hurt­ing any­body, and only where it can ac­tu­ally suc­ceed.
That was the tool­kit Amit Varma and Ajay Shah built[[x1]] in this episode, pick­ing up from their last one on the state.

The state is al­ways co­er­cive, Varma re­called, and it pays for ev­ery­thing with taxes it takes by force. So every pro­posal that it act must be jus­ti­fied. “Each time we are jus­ti­fy­ing vi­o­lence[[x2]],” he said. {026-C01}
The hard part is draw­ing the lines with­out it be­com­ing, in Shah’s words, “your phi­los­o­phy ver­sus mine”.
## A lunch that is free

Economists, Shah said, have built a frame­work for this. Freedom is the base­line. Then there is a nar­row class of prob­lems, called mar­ket fail­ure, where “the cor­rect kind of state in­ter­ven­tion is a free lunch be­cause it will make some peo­ple in so­ci­ety bet­ter off with­out harm­ing any­body at all”. {026-C03}
That makes it com­mon ground. “We’re not doing Robin Hood,” Shah said. It is not about tak­ing from the rich, and it does not ig­nite class war­fare.
Market fail­ures come in four buck­ets: mar­ket power, ex­ter­nal­i­ties, asym­met­ric in­for­ma­tion and pub­lic goods. Outside them, free­dom stays the de­fault.
## Hold it there
Spotting a mar­ket fail­ure only starts the con­ver­sa­tion. “Do not rush in where an­gels fear to tread,” Shah said. {#angels}
Very many times, he said, the state marches into some­thing and it be­comes a mess. So be­fore in­ter­ven­ing, ask how hard the job will be.
For that he of­fered a test sim­ple enough for a con­ver­sa­tion over chai. Lant Pritchett and Michael Woolcock posed two ques­tions in a 2004 paper; Shah and Vijay Kelkar added two more.
Are there many trans­ac­tions? Do front­line staff have dis­cre­tion? Are the stakes high? Is there se­crecy? Four yes-or-no an­swers tell you whether a prob­lem is easy or hard. {026-C12}
A polio drive is easy: many trans­ac­tions, but no dis­cre­tion. Criminal jus­tice is hard: the ac­cused faces jail, and “the dan­gers of cor­rup­tion and dis­cre­tion just go to in­fin­ity”.

Among the ways to fix a prob­lem, Shah said, pick the least in­tru­sive, and go to the root cause: when the air is bad, “don’t build hos­pi­tals”. Each prob­lem, too, be­longs at the low­est level of gov­ern­ment that can take it.
And some­times the an­swer is to walk away. A bad in­ter­ven­tion, Shah said, can be worse than liv­ing with the mar­ket fail­ure it claims to fix.
## A slow ap­pren­tice­ship
No state learns all this overnight. Europe’s states, Shah said, spent cen­turies mostly rais­ing taxes and wag­ing war, and learned in the process how to be a state.
India, he ar­gued, should start with a very low scope, the po­lice and the ju­di­ciary, and for one or two gen­er­a­tions learn how to do those few things. {026-C16}
Arguing over more wel­fare or less, he said, is not use­ful while such basic prob­lems burn.

Varma, cit­ing the writer Johan Norberg, said the Nordic coun­tries got rich as free-market economies be­fore they built wel­fare states. Copy one Swedish out­come, Shah warned, and you need Swedish rule of law be­hind it.
“It’s not an NGO, it’s not a nice guy, it’s not a mother,” Shah said of the state. “It’s a co­er­cive crea­ture with its own self-interest.”

second.label: Public goods
second.head: Clean air, by drone
second.deck: Ajay Shah on what a public good really is, and what it isn’t

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the public good of clean air

body: A pub­lic good is not any­thing that hap­pens to be good for the pub­lic, Ajay Shah said. Technically, it is non-rival and non-excludable[[x3]]. {026-C05}

One young woman walk­ing safely down a street does not use up its safety, and no one could, even in the­ory, ex­clude a new­born child from breath­ing clean air. So the pol­lu­tion over North India is a true pub­lic-goods prob­lem.

Shah would back taxes to put 10,000 drones over the Hindi heart­land[[x4]], find every fire and ticket who­ever lit it. {#drones} India’s so-called dig­i­tal pub­lic goods, by con­trast, are gen­er­ally rival and ex­clud­able, he said.

quote.text: The wel­fareist so­cial­ist im­pulse in India is any­thing that is good for the peo­ple is a pub­lic good, and that’s just wrong.

third.head: Friendly to whom?

pic.caption: Amit Varma on business-friendly and market-friendly

body: People as­sume that busi­ness-friendly means mar­ket-friendly[[x5]], Amit Varma said. “They’re ab­so­lutely the op­po­site.” {026-C09}

Market-friendly means com­pe­ti­tion and free entry, which serves con­sumers. Business-friendly means look­ing after the busi­nesses al­ready there, which want to keep com­peti­tors out. Every big busi­ness wants to be a mo­nop­oly, he said, and lob­bies the gov­ern­ment for tar­iffs and reg­u­la­tions.

Genuine mo­nop­o­lies, Varma ar­gued, are in­cred­i­bly rare[[x6]] in a com­pet­i­tive mar­ket­place. Look closely at one and you usu­ally find crony­ism, or a state that has blocked entry in some way. Or it is not a mo­nop­oly at all, and some­one has de­fined it wrongly.

Ajay Shah, for his part, warned against the pop­ulist urge to pun­ish mo­nop­o­lists out of envy. A nat­u­ral mo­nop­oly, he said, may need only its prices reg­u­lated, not to be bro­ken up. {#natural}

p2.deck: Market failure, four hard questions and a good deal of patience: when, the hosts asked, should the state act?

quote.text: It’s very im­por­tant to note we’re not doing pop­ulism. We’re not tak­ing money from the rich and giv­ing it to the poor.

box.title: The book behind the toolkit
box.text: Market fail­ure, the ex­tended test of dif­fi­culty and the least in­tru­sive in­ter­ven­tion all come from *In Service of the Republic*[[x10]] by Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah. Amit Varma calls it “a mas­ter­piece avail­able to you at your near­est book­store”. {026-R03}

sections.label: First principles
sections.head: Some better off, none worse
sections.caption: market failure and its four buckets
body: Amit Varma first re­called where the hosts stood: the state is al­ways co­er­cive, and India “hap­pens to have a weak state that does too much”. {026-C02}
Ajay Shah took it from there. Freedom is the base­line[[x12]]: human be­ings, he said, “should swing their arms wildly and not be con­strained by a boom arm re­quired by a gov­ern­ment reg­u­la­tor”.

Then there is a nar­row class of prob­lems, called mar­ket fail­ure[[x11]], where the right in­ter­ven­tion makes some peo­ple bet­ter off with­out harm­ing any­body. That, Shah ar­gued, is a tech­ni­cal core ev­ery­one can agree on, with no Robin Hood and no class war­fare. {026-C03}
## Four buck­ets
The first bucket is mar­ket power. Even a mo­nop­oly, he said, should be han­dled in ways the mo­nop­o­list could sign on to, not out of envy and re­sent­ment.

The sec­ond is ex­ter­nal­i­ties, spillovers no­body con­tracted for. If I get vac­ci­nated, you are bet­ter off, so I un­der­in­vest; if I play loud­speak­ers, I de­stroy your peace. “My free­dom to move my fist should be lim­ited not just by the ab­sence of the boom arm, but by the prox­im­ity of your nose.”
The third is asym­met­ric in­for­ma­tion: grand­moth­ers and den­tists can­not tell whether a bank is sound. Google gut­ter oil, Shah urged: “It will blow your mind.” {026-J05}
~ The fourth is pub­lic goods, such as clean air. Outside these four, free­dom stays the de­fault. “These are green lighted by the econ­o­mists as mar­ket fail­ure,” Shah said. {026-C04}

quote.text: It’s very im­por­tant to note we’re not doing pop­ulism. We’re not tak­ing money from the rich and giv­ing it to the poor.

sections.label: The caveats
sections.head: Where is the coercion?
sections.caption: the high bar of proof
body: Amit Varma agreed with the frame­work en­tirely, then added his warn­ings. To say that free­dom “doesn’t quite work” some­where is a util­i­tar­ian claim about con­se­quences, he said.

“One of my is­sues with all util­i­tar­ian think­ing is that it as­sumes that knowl­edge is easy,” he said. “Knowledge is not easy.” Thinkers with an en­gi­neer­ing mind­set pre­dict that if we do this, that will hap­pen, and none of it hap­pens. {026-C07}
People cite mar­ket fail­ure to jus­tify state in­ter­ven­tion, he added, but no one talks of state fail­ure[[x13]], which pub­lic choice the­ory shows to be prac­ti­cally ubiq­ui­tous.
## Plain words, fine print

Language mud­dies things too. Not find­ing a green cush­ion in a shop of blue ones, Varma said, is no mar­ket fail­ure. Ajay Shah called it the bane of his field that eco­nom­ics re­pur­poses plain English words, un­like sci­ence and math­e­mat­ics. {026-C06}
Varma’s own test is four words long. Faced with any prob­lem in so­ci­ety, he asks: “Where is the co­er­cion?” In his case, he said, that is al­ways where the root lies. {026-C10}
~ Even an ap­par­ent mo­nop­oly, he ar­gued, usu­ally turns out to be de­fined wrongly or propped up by the state.

quote.text: The bar of proof should be very high. It should not be some­thing that you can use con­ve­niently to crush free­dom

art.caption: Ajay Shah on the high bar of proof

sections.label: The difficulty test
sections.head: Four questions over chai
sections.caption: how hard an intervention will be
body: “Just be­cause there’s a mar­ket fail­ure, it doesn’t mean that a state in­ter­ven­tion will suc­ceed,” Ajay Shah said. So be­fore act­ing, ask how hard the bat­tle will be[[x15]].

He wanted a test sim­ple enough for every draw­ing room in the coun­try, one the “great dic­ta­tor Amit Bhai” could apply over chai. The first two ques­tions come from a 2004 paper by Lant Pritchett and Michael Woolcock[[x14]]. {026-R07}
Are there many trans­ac­tions? Do front­line staff have dis­cre­tion? Shah and Vijay Kelkar added two: are the stakes high, and is there se­crecy?
## Easy drops, hard cases
A polio drive has many trans­ac­tions but no dis­cre­tion. Staff walk into a slum or vil­lage, put the drop on ev­ery­one and fol­low a man­ual, so it rolls out eas­ily.

A teacher who skips her gov­ern­ment school steals ₹15,000 a month, so the ef­fort put into mis­be­haviour is lim­ited. {#teacher} But when the ac­cused in a crim­i­nal case faces jail, the stakes are sky high, and so is the pull to­wards cor­rup­tion.
Secrecy hides fail­ure. The mil­i­tary is ad­mired, Shah said, but its se­crecy is likely cover for a lot of state fail­ure. {026-S03}
~ Four yes-or-no an­swers, he said, tell you straight away whether you face an easy prob­lem or a hard one. {026-C12}

quote.text: In these four zero one num­bers, you’ve got a grip of the essence that some things are easy, some things are hard

sections.label: The lightest touch
sections.head: Knock, but don’t come in
sections.caption: the least intrusive intervention
body: If there are ten ways to in­ter­vene, choose the least op­pres­sive, Amit Varma said, re­mind­ing Ajay Shah of a point from the book Shah wrote with Vijay Kelkar.

Shah agreed. “A good in­ter­ven­tion is one that is the least in­tru­sive in the lives of peo­ple[[x16]],” he said. The lib­eral dream is to live on your own terms, with­out need­ing to think about the state at all. {026-C13}
He sketched some rules. Touching a human body is worse than not touch­ing it; knock­ing on a door is worse than not knock­ing; en­ter­ing a house is worse than stand­ing at the door.
The cheap­est fix, he added, is at the root cause: build good roads rather than a trauma cen­tre at every high­way exit.
## Closer to home

Varma ar­gued for gov­ern­ment that is as local as pos­si­ble. Kerala’s prob­lem is di­a­betes and obe­sity, Bihar’s is mal­nour­ish­ment, yet cen­tral schemes are de­signed in Delhi around the prob­lems nearby. {026-S04}

Shah named the idea: the sub­sidiar­ity prin­ci­ple, which places every prob­lem at the low­est level of gov­ern­ment where it can be placed. {026-C14} He called it one of the great ideas in eco­nom­ics, prompt­ing Varma to ask how many there were.
~ You don’t al­ways have to do some­thing, Varma said: gov­ern­ment “has lim­ited ca­pac­ity, lim­ited money, lim­ited band­width”. {026-C15}

quote.text: Living with a mar­ket fail­ure is often bet­ter than liv­ing with a bad state in­ter­ven­tion that claims to ad­dress that mar­ket fail­ure

art.caption: Ajay Shah on the least intrusive intervention

sections.label: Learning by doing
sections.head: Sweden wasn’t built in a day
sections.caption: how states learn to be states
body: Did the im­mense scope of the Swedish state emerge pris­tine into the world? “Of course not,” Ajay Shah said. Nobody can build the Swedish state overnight.
In Europe in the 17th, 18th and 19th cen­turies, he said, states mostly raised taxes and waged war. “It took hun­dreds of years, but around that, they learned how to be a state.” {026-S02}
So it is al­ways wise to start with a very low scope[[x18]], Shah ar­gued, and spend one or two gen­er­a­tions learn­ing to do a few nar­row things. {026-C16}

For India, he means ba­sics like the po­lice and the ju­di­ciary. “For 25 years, for 50 years, we have to learn how to do ba­sics,” he said. {#basics} Only then should so­ci­ety de­bate widen­ing the state’s scope.
## The Nordic ques­tion

Amit Varma took on the fa­mil­iar re­tort about Scandinavia[[x17]]. Behind their wel­fare states, he said, the Nordic coun­tries keep great in­di­vid­ual lib­erty, and start­ing a busi­ness there is far eas­ier than in India.
They also be­came rich be­fore they be­came wel­fare states. The writer Johan Norberg, Varma said, shows that they were model free-market economies first. {026-R15}
~ Shah added that one Swedish re­sult can­not be copied with­out the rest: “Swedish lev­els of the cash­less econ­omy is backed by Swedish lev­els of rule of law.” {026-C17}

quote.text: So it’s al­ways wise to start with a very low scope, start with a few nar­row prob­lems

As a card car­ry­ing econ­o­mist, I’m say­ing to you that so­ci­eties flour­ish when free­dom is a base­line and gov­ern­ment in­ter­ven­tion is lim­ited to the class of mar­ket fail­ures where there can be a suc­cess­ful im­ple­men­ta­tion.

p3.title: Tales of the state
p3.deck: Four stories the hosts told, from Bollywood’s colour grading to Russia’s army

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on how the means of production got cheap
stories.head: Hollywood colour, laptop price
body: Ajay Shah opened the episode smil­ing. The clunky boom arms were gone, re­placed by new wire­less mi­cro­phones from Rode that record audio in 32-bit float. “We’ve got a new level of human free­dom,” Shah said. “We can wave our arms around.” {026-R19}

Amit Varma, who feared that one day he would dis­ap­pear and Shah would be even hap­pier, likened 32-bit float to RAW in pho­tog­ra­phy: ev­ery­thing is cap­tured, so the lev­els can be fixed later. {#raw}

Shah saw a German philoso­pher in all this: the pro­le­tariat own­ing the means of pro­duc­tion. “You and I, hum­ble slaves and pro­duc­ers, are no longer the sub­jects of the giant media com­pa­nies,” he said. Varma had guessed Immanuel Kant; the ex­change ended on a pun: “Now Immanuel can.” {026-J02}

Then Varma told his favourite story about the means of pro­duc­tion. DaVinci Resolve is today one of the big three edit­ing pro­grams. Anyone can down­load it free, and the free ver­sion gives state-of-the-art edit­ing and the best colour grad­ing.
It was not al­ways so. Back in 2010, when it did only colour grad­ing, Varma asked Shah to guess the price. {#grading} Shah ven­tured that it was more than most Indian media com­pa­nies would pay.
“There wasn’t one in India be­cause it cost eight hun­dred thou­sand dol­lars for colour grad­ing,” Varma said. {026-S01}
~ So Bollywood films were sent to Hollywood for colour grad­ing and shipped back, with the rental part of the cost. Varma called the change “ut­terly mirac­u­lous”.
stories.why: In about a decade, a tool only a few stu­dios could af­ford be­came free. The means of pro­duc­tion now sit with in­di­vid­ual cre­ators, which is what lets two peo­ple make their own show.
stories.postscript: Shah’s shirt came from Indian Colours, which li­censes Indian artists’ work and pays them roy­al­ties, much as au­thors earn on books.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the $800,000 colour-grading software

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how European states learned their trade
stories.head: Tax, fight, repeat
body: Sweden’s vast state did not spring up overnight, Ajay Shah said. In every ad­vanced econ­omy, learn­ing to run a state cor­rectly took hun­dreds of years. {026-C16}

In Europe in the 17th, 18th and 19th cen­turies, states did es­sen­tially two things. They ran a fis­cal sys­tem to raise taxes, the so-called fis­cus, and they waged war, with all the con­tract­ing[[x19]] and tech­nol­ogy that arms re­quired. {026-S02}

Doing those nar­row jobs over and over, they learned HR, con­tract­ing, checks and bal­ances[[x20]] and how to con­trol cor­rup­tion. They learned to solve prin­ci­pal-agent prob­lems, and to keep the mil­i­tary in its bar­racks in­side a lib­eral democ­racy.
~ Only then, Shah said, were those hard-won lessons ap­plied to new prob­lems, such as vac­cines.

quote.text: It took hun­dreds of years, but around that, they learned how to be a state.

stories.postscript: Shah’s pre­scrip­tion for India: 25 to 50 years of learn­ing the ba­sics, such as the po­lice and the ju­di­ciary. {#basics}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on how Europe learned to be a state

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on what Delhi’s schemes miss
stories.head: Kerala’s sugar, Bihar’s hunger
body: Amit Varma took his ex­am­ple from two of his own con­ver­sa­tions: one with Pranay Kotasthane on cen­trally spon­sored schemes, and one with RS Nilakantan about his book on South India. {026-S04}

The needs of the North and the South, he said, are very dif­fer­ent. Kerala has a prob­lem of di­a­betes and obe­sity[[x21]]. Bihar, like other parts of north and cen­tral India, strug­gles with mal­nour­ish­ment.

Ideally, each state would get a health bud­get and de­cide lo­cally how best to tackle its own prob­lem. Instead, cen­tral schemes are de­signed in Delhi, for the nearby prob­lem, and miss local needs. {026-R11}
~ Ajay Shah sup­plied the name for the cure: the sub­sidiar­ity prin­ci­ple[[x22]], which places every prob­lem at the low­est level of gov­ern­ment where it can be placed. {026-C14}

quote.text: The needs of the North and the South are so dif­fer­ent. But the pri­or­i­ties of the North dic­tate pub­lic pol­icy.

stories.postscript: Varma, mid-story, plugged the hosts’ di­a­betes episode: “We can con­quer di­a­betes. Yes, we can.”

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Kerala’s diabetes and Bihar’s hunger

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on secrecy as a cover for failure
stories.head: Secrets behind the pomp
body: Secrecy is the fourth ques­tion in Ajay Shah’s test of dif­fi­culty, and his ex­am­ple was an in­sti­tu­tion held in high re­gard: the mil­i­tary. {026-S03}

“While there is a lot of ad­mi­ra­tion and re­spect for the mil­i­tary, it is also the case that the mil­i­tary is shrouded in se­crecy,” he said. That se­crecy, he ar­gued, is likely cover for a lot of state fail­ure.

Once the shoot­ing started in Putin’s war, the world found “mind-blowing fail­ures”[[x23]] in­side the Russian mil­i­tary. {#putin} They had been cov­ered up by pompous pa­rades, na­tion­al­ism and mil­i­tarism.
~ Where a gov­ern­ment ac­tiv­ity runs under com­plete trans­parency, Shah said, more peo­ple no­tice mis­be­haviour and malfea­sance, and there is more check and bal­ance.
stories.why: A grand spec­ta­cle says noth­ing about whether an in­sti­tu­tion works. Secrecy re­moves the scru­tiny that ex­poses malfea­sance, so the most opaque parts of the state tend to hide the most fail­ure.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on military secrecy and Russia’s failures

quiz.q: What, in the technical sense, makes something a public good, according to Ajay Shah?
quiz.a: It is non-rival and non-excludable, like clean air, not merely good for the pub­lic.

quiz.q: Name the four buckets of market failure that economists green-light for state intervention.
quiz.a: Market power, ex­ter­nal­i­ties, asym­met­ric in­for­ma­tion and pub­lic goods; out­side them, free­dom stays the de­fault.

quiz.q: Why is a polio drive an easy problem for the state, by Shah’s test?
quiz.a: Many trans­ac­tions, but no dis­cre­tion: front­line staff sim­ply fol­low a man­ual and give the drops.

quiz.q: What principle places every problem at the lowest level of government that can handle it?
quiz.a: The sub­sidiar­ity prin­ci­ple, which Ajay Shah called one of the great ideas in eco­nom­ics.

quiz.q: What did DaVinci Resolve cost in 2010, when it only did colour grading?
quiz.a: Eight hun­dred thou­sand dol­lars, so India had no copy and films went to Hollywood.

quiz.q: According to Amit Varma, what did the Nordic countries become before they became welfare states?
quiz.a: Rich, as model free-market economies, as the writer Johan Norberg de­scribes in de­tail.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 26. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Johan Norberg (Krubaston, CC0); Vijay Kelkar (Press Information Bureau, Government of India, GODL-India); James C. Scott (SOAS University of London, CC BY 3.0); Francis Fukuyama (Gobierno de Chile, CC BY 2.0); Shaun Tan (K Tempest Bradford from New York City, CC BY 2.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon, Open Library and Wikipedia.

shelf.title: Seeing Like a State: How Certain Schemes to Improve the Human Condition Have Failed
shelf.creator: James C Scott
shelf.why: Scott’s ac­count of how state schemes to im­prove the human con­di­tion fail when bu­reau­cra­cies can­not ‘see’ the so­ci­ety they rule, with a tool­kit (state leg­i­bil­ity, high mod­ernism, metis) you can apply al­most any­where.

shelf.title: Cicada
shelf.creator: Shaun Tan
shelf.why: Amit calls Shaun Tan a great il­lus­tra­tor, writer and artist and the book ‘marvelous’.

shelf.title: In Service of the Republic
shelf.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ frame­work for Indian eco­nomic pol­icy: when the state should step in, why its fail­ures cut across every do­main (HR, con­tract­ing, bud­get­ing, checks on co­er­cive power), and why the fix is checks and bal­ances and small, re­versible steps.

shelf.title: The Art and Science of Economic Policy (Episode 154 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A long con­ver­sa­tion with Vijay Kelkar and Ajay about their book In Service of the Republic and its frame­work for eco­nomic pol­icy.

shelf.title: State Building
shelf.creator: Francis Fukuyama
shelf.why: A slim book that re­places the vague ‘big state ver­sus small state’ de­bate with two di­men­sions: how much a state tries to do and how well it does it.

shelf.title: Understanding the State (Episode 25)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The foun­da­tion of the show’s think­ing on gov­ern­ment: the state is a mo­nop­oly on vi­o­lence that acts through co­er­cion, so every in­ter­ven­tion, paid for by taxes, must be jus­ti­fied.

shelf.title: Solutions When the Solution is the Problem: Arraying the Disarray in Development
shelf.creator: Lant Pritchett and Michael Woolcock
shelf.why: Pritchett and Woolcock ask whether an in­ter­ven­tion is easy or hard to im­ple­ment, a ques­tion Ajay calls a break­through that Indian pol­icy de­bate rarely asks: in­ter­ven­tions with many trans­ac­tions or much dis­cre­tion for front­line staff are harder to de­liver.

shelf.title: Ajay Shah on the Dangers of Digital Public Infrastructure (Episode 72 of Brave New World)
shelf.creator: Vasant Dhar
shelf.why: Ajay on Vasant Dhar’s pod­cast, lay­ing out his fun­da­men­tal ob­jec­tion to India’s so-called ‘dig­i­tal pub­lic goods’: by the strict def­i­ni­tion they are gen­er­ally rival and ex­clud­able, so they are not pub­lic goods at all.

shelf.title: Public Choice: A Primer
shelf.creator: Eomonn Butler
shelf.why: A short, mas­ter­ful in­tro­duc­tion to pub­lic choice the­ory, read­able in under an hour, that ex­plains why state fail­ure is prac­ti­cally ev­ery­where though ev­ery­one talks only of mar­ket fail­ure.

shelf.title: Amit Varma on Public Choice Theory (mashup of The Seen and the Unseen and The Pragati Podcast)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: An audio in­tro­duc­tion to the field Amit says ex­plains why state fail­ure is ubiq­ui­tous.

shelf.title: Centrally Sponsored Government Schemes (Episode 20 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Pranay Kotasthane
shelf.why: Pranay Kotasthane on how schemes de­signed in Delhi fail to fit the very dif­fer­ent needs of India’s states and work as a back­door for cen­tral con­trol over state sub­jects.

shelf.title: South India Would Like to Have a Word (Episode 320 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with RS Nilakantan
shelf.why: RS Nilakantan on how dif­fer­ently South India’s needs look from the North’s, though the North’s pri­or­i­ties drive na­tional pol­icy, and on the North-South dis­par­i­ties be­hind that.

shelf.title: How I Reversed My Type 2 Diabetes (Episode 9)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit’s ac­count of re­vers­ing his di­a­betes through diet: eat less ce­real, avoid pro­cessed food, and treat ghee as a su­per­food and sugar as poi­son.

shelf.title: Yes Minister / Yes Prime Minister
shelf.creator: Jonathan Lynn and Antony Jay
shelf.why: It sup­plies the per­fect par­ody of pol­icy re­flexes, ‘We must do some­thing, this is some­thing, there­fore we must do this.’

shelf.title: Johan Norberg’s writings on Sweden’s free-market rise
shelf.creator: Johan Norberg
shelf.why: Norberg shows in de­tail that the Nordic coun­tries got rich as free-market economies first and built their wel­fare states af­ter­wards: Amit’s an­swer to peo­ple who cite Scandinavia against the case for free­dom.

shelf.title: Indian Colours
shelf.why: The source of many of Ajay’s art shirts: it prints con­tem­po­rary Indian art on shirts, cups and stoles and pays artists roy­al­ties, so or­di­nary peo­ple can sur­round them­selves with beauty with­out spend­ing lakhs on orig­i­nals.

shelf.title: DaVinci Resolve
shelf.why: The free ver­sion alone gives you state-of-the-art edit­ing and the best colour grad­ing, from soft­ware that once cost $800,000.

shelf.title: $800,000 to Zero - The FASCINATING History of DaVinci Resolve
shelf.creator: Learn Color Grading
shelf.why: Amit calls it a great video on how a once-unaffordable pro­fes­sional tool be­came free.

shelf.title: RODE Wireless PRO
shelf.creator: RODE
shelf.why: Microphones that record 32-bit float audio, which Amit calls mirac­u­lous: like RAW for pho­to­graphs, it cap­tures ev­ery­thing, so sound never clips and lev­els can be fixed af­ter­wards.

shelf.title: How 32-bit Float Recording Works on the Wireless PRO
shelf.why: For any­one cu­ri­ous about the tech­nol­ogy Ajay ad­mits he ‘only dimly’ un­der­stands.

shelf.title: The RODE Wireless PRO is NUTS!
shelf.creator: DLSR Video Shooter
shelf.why: A hands-on re­view of the gear be­hind the hosts’ new ‘level of human freedom’.

shelf.title: Pune Public Policy Festival (January 19-20, 2024)
shelf.why: A fes­ti­val (and the show’s spon­sor) that brings young pro­fes­sion­als to­gether with bu­reau­crats, econ­o­mists and thinkers to de­bate trade-offs such as en­vi­ron­ment ver­sus growth and tech­nol­ogy ver­sus pri­vacy; Amit likes that it pulls pol­icy dis­cus­sion back to Pune, once called the Oxford of the East.

shelf.title: Why Freedom Matters (Episode 10)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Despite the title, an eco­nomic his­tory of India told through the lens of free­dom: the boom after 1869, Nehru’s Fabian so­cial­ism, the lost years from the 1962 war to the Emergency, and the open­ing-up that lifted mil­lions out of poverty.

laughs.text: Opening on Ajay’s big smile after the clunky boom arms were re­moved: ‘I have the feel­ing one day I will dis­ap­pear and you will be even hap­pier.’ (Amit)

The German philoso­pher mix-up. Amit is told he missed a chance to plug a German philoso­pher and asks what Immanuel Kant’s cat­e­gor­i­cal im­per­a­tive has to do with it. Ajay means the pro­le­tariat own­ing the means of pro­duc­tion: ‘So you and I, hum­ble slaves and pro­duc­ers, are no longer the sub­jects of the giant media com­pa­nies.’ The ex­change lands on the pun that names the chap­ter: ‘Who says Immanuel can’t? Now Immanuel can.’

The boom-arm run­ning gag. Ajay says the new mics give ‘a new level of human free­dom. We can wave our arms around.’ He then builds it into the eco­nom­ics: by de­fault peo­ple should ‘swing their arms wildly and not be con­strained by a boom arm re­quired by a gov­ern­ment reg­u­la­tor.’ On ex­ter­nal­i­ties: ‘my free­dom to move my fist should be lim­ited not just by the ab­sence of the boom arm, but by the prox­im­ity of your nose.’

Ajay on food safety: ‘Gentle reader, please Google gut­ter oil. It will blow your mind.’ Amit, judg­ing only from Ajay’s face: ‘I sus­pect it will blow your guts as well. ... don’t tell me, don’t tell me, con­tinue.’
Yes Minister / Yes Prime Minister (Jonathan Lynn and Antony Jay), quoted for the policymaker’s fal­lacy: ‘we must do some­thing, this is some­thing, there­fore we must do this.’
